Accommodation. Village pensions are small; book ahead in spring. Many will send your bag on to the next stop for a fee.
Alcohol is widely available in cities and on the coasts, less so in conservative towns. Many restaurants in the east and southeast don’t serve it.

Avoid prayer times. Visitors are usually asked to leave or wait during the five daily prayers, which last around 20–30 minutes. Friday midday prayer is the busiest of the week; plan to visit later in the afternoon.
Be discreet. Eating, drinking and smoking in public isn’t forbidden for visitors, but doing it quietly is a kindness, especially in conservative areas.
Before dawn in some neighbourhoods a drummer walks the streets to wake people for sahur, the pre-dawn meal.
Cheese. Usually white beyaz peynir and yellow kaşar; in Van, otlu peynir flavoured with wild herbs.
Dress modestly. Shoulders and knees covered for everyone. Women cover their hair; large mosques usually lend scarves and wraps at the door, but carrying a light scarf is easier.
Eggs. Menemen (scrambled with tomato and pepper) or sucuklu yumurta with spiced sausage.
Follow the signs. Some areas are for worshippers only, and in some mosques visitors use a separate entrance.
Honey and kaymak. A clotted cream eaten with honey on bread. One of the great pleasures of the country.
Iftar, the meal that breaks the fast at sunset, is a lovely time to be out. Squares fill with families, and restaurants are full, so book or eat early.
Kahvaltı, breakfast, is a spread of small plates: cheeses, olives, tomatoes, cucumbers, honey and kaymak, eggs, and bread. Read our guide to the Turkish breakfast.
Keep your voice low and don’t walk directly in front of anyone praying.
Late cancellations. Sometimes you’ll be collected, driven to the launch field and then sent back because conditions changed. That is the system working.
Lokanta are workers’ restaurants with ready-cooked dishes on display: point at what you want. Usually lunch only, often the best food in town.

The holiday that follows, Ramazan Bayramı (Eid al-Fitr), is a public holiday of several days. Buses, flights and hotels fill up as families travel, and some offices and museums change their hours. Book well ahead.

Turkish coffee is boiled with the grounds in a small pot and served thick, usually after a meal. Say how sweet you’d like it when you order: sade (plain), orta (medium) or şekerli (sweet). Don’t drink the grounds.
Vegetarians eat well with meze, zeytinyağlı dishes, lentil soup and pide, but check: “etsiz” means without meat. Many vegetable dishes are cooked with meat stock.
Water. Springs and cisterns can be dry. Carry at least two litres, more on long climbs.

Balloon flights in Cappadocia depend on the wind, and the decision to fly is made early each morning. It is not unusual for flights to be cancelled several days in a row, especially in winter. Someone who has planned one night in Göreme can easily go home without flying.

Balloons can fly in every month, but the odds change with the seasons. Spring and autumn generally have the most settled mornings. Winter brings more wind, snow and cloud, and more cancellations, though the snowy flights that do go are spectacular.

Capital of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rûm, which built most of Anatolia’s caravanserais to draw trade across its lands. It is also the city of Rumi, the poet whose followers became the whirling dervishes. His tomb is now the Mevlana Museum.

Cappadocia sits on the old caravan road between Konya and Kayseri, and two of the finest Seljuk caravanserais, Sultanhanı near Aksaray and Saruhan near Avanos, are within reach. The landscape itself is volcanic ash compressed into tuff, soft enough to carve and hard enough to last.

Caravans from Tabriz crossed the Pontic mountains to reach the sea here. Trabzon was the capital of its own small Byzantine empire, rich enough to commission the frescoes still visible in its Hagia Sophia.

Ephesus is the most complete Roman city in the eastern Mediterranean: a marble street running downhill past the Library of Celsus to a theatre that once held around 25,000 people. Arrive at opening time or late in the afternoon, and allow extra for the Terrace Houses, whose painted walls and mosaics are under a protective roof.

Every morning the Turkish civil aviation authority (SHGM), which has an office in Göreme, checks the weather and makes one decision for the whole region, shown as a coloured flag: green means balloons may fly, red means they are grounded. Individual operators cannot overrule a red flag, and even on a green day the pilot may still decide not to go.

From the thirteenth century the Seljuk sultans built stone caravanserais along Anatolia’s trade roads, roughly a day’s march apart. Silk, spices and news travelled between Persia, Mesopotamia and the ports. Many of the inns still stand.
Gaziantep’s pistachio baklava and kebabs; Urfa’s smoky isot pepper, lahmacun and çiğ köfte; Mardin’s içli köfte and stuffed lamb ribs. The most exciting cooking in the country.

Göbekli Tepe, near Şanlıurfa, rewrote the story of early civilisation: circles of carved stone pillars put up by hunter-gatherers more than 11,000 years ago, before pottery or writing. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2018, protective roofs now cover the main enclosures, and the Şanlıurfa museum complex shows finds and a reconstruction of one enclosure.

Lake Van sits at around 1,640 metres, ringed by volcanoes. It has no outflow and its water is salty and strongly alkaline (a soda lake), so few fish live in it, and the colour shifts from deep blue to green with the light. The region was the heart of the ancient kingdom of Urartu and later of medieval Armenian kingdoms.

Mardin climbs a hillside above the plain that runs south into Syria. Its stone houses, madrasas and Syriac churches are a reminder that this has long been a place of many faiths and languages. Nearby Midyat and the Tur Abdin plateau have working Syriac Orthodox monasteries, including Mor Gabriel.

Mosques in Türkiye are working places of prayer, and most welcome visitors. A little preparation shows respect and makes the visit easier for everyone.
Most visitors come for one day. Stay three: the boat to Akdamar Island, the lakeside Seljuk cemetery at Ahlat, the Urartian citadel at Van, and a long breakfast in between.

Most visitors stay within the old peninsula of Sultanahmet. We suggest spending at least as much time across the water: in Kadıköy’s food market on the Asian shore, on the ferries that cost less than a coffee, and in the steep lanes of Balat and Fener on the Golden Horn.

Pamukkale means “cotton castle”: calcium-rich spring water has built white terraces down the hillside over thousands of years. You walk them barefoot, on a set path, to protect the surface.

Pergamon, at Bergama to the north, is less visited and more dramatic: a royal acropolis on a ridge, with one of the steepest theatres in the ancient world cut into the hillside. Below it are the Asklepion, an ancient healing centre, and the Red Basilica.

Ramadan (Ramazan in Turkish) is the month of fasting from dawn to sunset. Practice varies a lot across Türkiye: in İstanbul and on the coasts daily life barely changes, while in more traditional towns, especially in the east and southeast, many people fast.

Ramadan moves about eleven days earlier each year, following the lunar calendar. In 2027 the first day of fasting is 8 February, and Ramazan Bayramı is 9–11 March, according to the Diyanet (Presidency of Religious Affairs) calendar. Kurban Bayramı (Eid al-Adha), another long holiday, is expected on 16–19 May 2027. Check the official calendar before you book.

The Turkish word is han, or kervansaray for the larger ones. A traveller would arrive at dusk, pass through a tall carved portal and find an enclosed world: a courtyard with a small mosque raised on arches in the middle, rooms around the edge, a bath, a blacksmith and a farrier for the animals. Behind the courtyard, the biggest hans have a covered hall with a forest of stone piers, for winter.

The balloons are almost as beautiful from the ground, and watching costs nothing. Find a viewpoint above Göreme or one of the valley ridges before sunrise and watch a hundred envelopes inflate and rise. Some cave hotels have roof terraces for exactly this.

The eastern Black Sea is unlike the rest of Türkiye: wet, forested mountains rising straight from the coast, with tea grown on terraces around Rize. Trabzon was the Black Sea port for caravans coming over the mountains from Tabriz and Persia.

The end of the road. Caravans unloaded in the great hans around the Grand Bazaar. Büyük Valide Han, built for Kösem Sultan in the mid-1600s, has three courtyards; Persian silk merchants once traded here, and some of its rooms are still workshops.
The famous Van breakfast of herb cheese, honey, kaymak and murtuğa, an egg-and-flour dish fried in butter, eaten over an entire morning.

The first Ottoman capital and the western end of the silk road. Koza Han, the “cocoon han”, was built for Bayezid II to fund his mosque in İstanbul, and for centuries it was the city’s market for silk cocoons. Its courtyard, around a small mosque raised on columns, is now full of silk shops and tea tables.

İstanbul was the end of the road for many Anatolian caravans. Goods came in through the hans around the Grand Bazaar, stone courtyards with rooms for merchants above and storerooms below, several still working today as tailors’ and coppersmiths’ workshops.

“Kervan” is Turkish for caravan. For centuries caravans of camels and mules carried silk, spices and news across Anatolia, resting each night at a caravanserai, a fortified inn built a day’s march from the last. We plan journeys at that pace.
